content: Continuing Medical Education (CME) is a specialized form of ongoing professional development (CPD) designed to maintain, enhance, or expand the knowledge, skills, professional performance, and interpersonal relationships that medical practitioners utilize in delivering care to patients, serving the public, or contributing to the medical profession. The scope of CME encompasses the foundational medical sciences, clinical medicine disciplines, and the delivery of healthcare services to the public, as recognized and accepted by the medical community. CME activities are educational interventions grounded in evidence-based medicine, aimed at addressing the educational needs of medical practitioners and ultimately improving patient care. These activities can be delivered through various formats, including live events, written publications, online programs, audio or video materials, and other electronic media. The content for these programs is developed, reviewed, and presented by faculty members who are experts in their respective clinical fields. To ensure transparency and integrity, any potential financial conflicts of interest involving faculty members must be disclosed and resolved appropriately, following a process similar to that used in academic journals. In 2005, there were 79,820 officially approved or accredited CME activities, a significant increase from 48,092 in 1998. Funding for CME activities is derived from diverse sources, including government agencies, private sector entities, managed care organizations, hospitals, academic institutions, non-profit organizations, and industry. Of this funding, $1.2 billion was attributed to commercial support. Two interactive formats commonly used in CME are case-based learning (CBL) and problem-based learning (PBL). Case-based learning employs a guided inquiry method and provides structured small-group sessions, while problem-based learning adopts an open inquiry approach with minimal instructor guidance. Research suggests that case-based learning may be more effective than other formats, and the use of multimedia can further enhance the delivery of educational content. CME is provided or facilitated by a variety of organizations, including government bodies, private non-profit professional societies, and academic institutions. Oversight of CME quality is critical to prevent commercial bias. To this end, the governing body of the CME enterprise has established and maintains Standards for Commercial Support to ensure the independence and quality of CME activities. Organizations such as the Alliance for CME, the largest professional organization for CME professionals, regularly convene meetings and events to address issues related to these standards and the evolution of the CME enterprise. Public media sources have occasionally scrutinized medical education practices. The Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME) oversees the allopathic CME enterprise, while osteopathic CME is governed by the Board of Trustees for CME of the American Osteopathic Association (AOA). The ACCME comprises seven member organizations and is tasked with identifying, developing, and promoting standards for high-quality CME. These standards are intended to help physicians maintain their competence and integrate new knowledge to improve the quality of medical care for patients and their communities. The ACCME fulfills its mission through a voluntary self-regulated system for accrediting CME providers and a peer-review process that adapts to changes in medical education and healthcare delivery systems. Many regulatory bodies require physicians to earn CME credits through accredited activities as a condition for maintaining their registration or licensure. Each state has its own specific CME requirements for physicians and other clinicians seeking to retain their licensure.
